questions.stem: According to the text, what is an agent?
options: A model that runs code independently without any feedback.
A model using tools in a loop.
A system that only runs code without any model involvement.
A system that only uses tools without any model.
questions.source_quote: An agent is a model using tools in a loop.

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the role of the harness in an agent system?
options: The harness is the model that makes decisions.
The harness is everything that is not the model, and it is where engineering happens.
The harness is a tool that runs the model's code.
The harness is a feedback loop that runs after the model.
questions.source_quote: The harness is everything that is not the model. It is deterministic code, and it is where engineering happens.

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the purpose of the feedback loop in an agent system?
options: To make the model run faster.
To check if the output meets the specification.
To let the model run without any checks.
To allow the model to run independently.
questions.source_quote: The feedback loop is around the whole agent. A check compares the output with the specification, and the error goes back in as the next input.

questions.stem: According to the text, who owns the control flow in an agent system?
options: The model.
The harness.
The user.
The feedback loop.
questions.source_quote: The model proposes. The harness decides.

questions.stem: According to the text, what is the difference between a loop and a graph in an agent system?
options: A loop is a way to run code faster, and a graph is for slower processes.
A loop is a single agent in a feedback loop, and a graph is a system of agents with known steps.
A loop is for testing, and a graph is for production.
A loop is for the model, and a graph is for the harness.
questions.source_quote: Loop: one agent inside one feedback loop. You give Claude Code a goal and a check, and it keeps going until the check passes. The model chooses every step in between. Graph: the work is split into steps that your code wires together.
